newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ National MPs to meet, but govt deal not ready.
newsitem.headline: NZ National MPs to meet, but govt deal not ready.

text.p: The ruling conservative National Party will hold a caucus meeting of MPs today but will not be considering a coalition deal, senior whip Roger Sowry said on Wednesday.
National postponed its regular caucus from Tuesday.

"No there won't be a deal (discussed today). Some of the media seem to think that we are miraculously going to have a deal at caucus. They fail to note that we actually haven't met NZ First face to face for a week," Sowry told Reuters.

Nationalist New Zealand First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and is negotiating separately with both National and the centre-left Labour Party over the shape of the next government.
Negotiations are almost complete and an announcement is expected next week, before the December 13 deadline for parliament to meet.
A spokesman for NZ First leader Winston Peters said things had advanced further. No meetings were planned today, although the parties continued to exchange reports by fax and telephone.
"No formal or informal meetings are scheduled at the moment, but if sufficient progress is made with the reports they could be called today," the spokesman said.
The National meeting follows meetings of the Labour and NZ First caucuses on Tuesday.

A report in the New Zealand Herald newspaper said National had agreed to defer a second round of tax cuts due on July 1, 1997 to cement a deal with NZ First. But Whangarei National MP John Banks said on his radio talkback show on Wednesday he would not go along with the National Party "cheating low and middle income-earners solemnly promised tax cuts", the New Zealand

A National-NZ First coalition would have 61 votes in the 120 seat parliament, although it could almost certainly rely on the single United Party MP Peter Dunne and the eight MPs of free- market Act New Zealand to support it if Banks rebelled.
Cancelling the cuts would give a future government an extra $1.1 billion to direct towards social spending of the sort advocated by NZ First during the election campaign.
Reserve Bank Governor Don Brash warned last month that coalition partners might need to consider deferring the cuts if they planned a net increase in government spending.
